q: Explain bias and variance in one sentence each.
a: Bias is error from a model too rigid to represent the truth; variance is how much the fitted model changes when you resample the training data.

q: Your training accuracy is 99% and validation is 72%. What now?
a: Classic overfitting: get more data, add regularisation or augmentation, reduce capacity, use early stopping — and first check for a leak or a distribution mismatch between the splits.

q: When is accuracy a misleading metric?
a: Whenever classes are imbalanced or error costs differ. At 99.9% negatives, predicting 'negative' always scores 99.9%. Use precision/recall at the deployed threshold, PR-AUC, or expected cost.

q: Difference between L1 and L2 regularisation.
a: L1 adds a constant-magnitude push toward zero so weights hit exactly zero (feature selection); L2's push is proportional to the weight so it shrinks smoothly without eliminating. Geometrically: the L1 constraint region has corners on the axes, the L2 ball does not.

q: Why is ROC-AUC unaffected by class imbalance, and when is that bad?
a: Both axes are within-class rates, so changing the negative count leaves them unchanged. That is bad at extreme imbalance: FPR barely moves even when almost every flagged case is a false alarm. Use precision-recall AUC.

q: What is the difference between bagging and boosting?
a: Bagging trains independent models on bootstrap samples in parallel and averages them — it reduces variance. Boosting trains models sequentially on the previous ensemble's errors — it reduces bias, and can overfit.

q: Explain the kernel trick.
a: Compute inner products in a high-dimensional feature space without ever constructing the mapping, by replacing the dot product with a kernel function. It makes non-linear separation tractable at the cost of an n×n Gram matrix.

q: How do you detect data leakage?
a: Suspiciously high offline metrics, a single feature with outsized importance, or a train/production gap. Check feature availability at prediction time, whether any transformation was fit before the split, and whether entity or time groups straddle folds.

q: Why does feature scaling matter, and for which models?
a: It matters for gradient-based and distance-based methods — linear/logistic regression, SVM, k-NN, k-means, PCA, neural nets — because the loss geometry and the distance metric depend on units. Tree-based models are invariant to monotone rescaling.

q: Explain precision and recall to a non-technical stakeholder.
a: Precision: of the cases we flagged, how many were real. Recall: of the real cases, how many we caught. Raising one usually lowers the other, so we pick the balance from the cost of each mistake.

q: When would you choose a simpler model over a more accurate one?
a: When the gain is within noise, when latency or cost budgets bind, when the decision must be explainable or auditable, when training data is small and unstable, or when the team has to maintain it at 3am.

q: What is the curse of dimensionality?
a: As dimensions grow, data becomes sparse and distances concentrate — the nearest and farthest neighbours become nearly equidistant, so distance-based methods and space-partitioning indexes degrade toward a full scan.

q: Explain cross-validation and when a simple k-fold is wrong.
a: k-fold rotates which fold is held out to get a lower-variance estimate. It is wrong when rows are not exchangeable: use group k-fold for repeated entities and time-based splits for forecasting.

q: What is a p-value, precisely?
a: The probability of observing data at least as extreme as yours, assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability the null is true, and not the probability your result is a fluke.

q: Explain the difference between generative and discriminative models.
a: Discriminative models learn P(y|x) directly (logistic regression, most classifiers). Generative models learn P(x,y) or P(x|y) and can sample new data (naive Bayes, GMMs, diffusion models, LLMs).

q: How do you handle missing data?
a: Understand the mechanism first — MCAR, MAR or MNAR. Then: drop if trivial and random, impute (median, model-based, or a learned indicator plus value), or use a model that handles nulls natively like LightGBM. Always add a missingness indicator when absence is informative.

q: What is the difference between correlation and causation in a feature?
a: A correlated feature predicts; a causal one changes the outcome when you intervene. Predictive models are fine with correlation, but any feature you might act on — or that reflects the current policy — needs causal reasoning or the model breaks on deployment.

q: Explain SHAP values.
a: A game-theoretic attribution: each feature's contribution is its average marginal effect over all orderings of the features. It is the unique attribution satisfying efficiency, symmetry, dummy and additivity — which is why it is preferred over ad-hoc importances.

q: Why do we need non-linear activations?
a: Because composing linear layers yields another linear layer, so depth adds no expressive power without a non-linearity between them.

q: What causes vanishing gradients and how do you fix it?
a: Gradients are products of per-layer Jacobians; if their typical scale is below 1 the product decays exponentially with depth. Fixes: residual connections, normalisation layers, ReLU-family activations, careful initialisation, and gating in recurrent models.

q: Batch norm vs layer norm — when do you use each?
a: BatchNorm normalises across the batch per feature: great for CNNs, but batch-dependent and awkward for variable-length sequences. LayerNorm normalises across features per example: batch-independent, identical in train and eval, which is why transformers use it.

q: What does dropout do at inference time?
a: Nothing — it is disabled. With inverted dropout, activations are scaled by 1/(1-p) during training so no test-time rescaling is needed. Forgetting model.eval() is the classic bug.

q: Adam vs SGD — when would you pick SGD?
a: SGD with momentum and a good schedule often generalises slightly better on vision benchmarks and uses a third of the optimiser memory. Adam wins when gradient scales vary wildly across parameters, which is the normal case in NLP.

q: Why decouple weight decay in AdamW?
a: In plain Adam, an L2 term in the loss is divided by the per-parameter second moment, so parameters with large gradients get less decay — the opposite of the intent. AdamW applies the decay directly to the weights instead.

q: How does gradient checkpointing work and what does it cost?
a: Store only a subset of activations in the forward pass and recompute the rest during backward. Memory drops roughly to the square root of layer count; compute rises about 30%.

q: What is the receptive field and how do you grow it?
a: The input region that influences one output unit. Grow it by stacking layers, increasing kernel size, striding, pooling, or using dilated convolutions — stacking small kernels is usually the cheapest.

q: Why do residual connections help?
a: They give the gradient an identity path, so the product of Jacobians always contains a 1 and cannot decay to zero. They also reframe each block as learning a residual correction, which is an easier function to fit than the full mapping.

q: What is mixed-precision training and why bf16 over fp16?
a: Compute in 16-bit with an fp32 master copy of the weights. bf16 has the same exponent range as fp32, so it rarely overflows and needs no loss scaling; fp16 has more mantissa bits but a narrow range that requires dynamic loss scaling.

q: How would you debug a model whose loss is NaN?
a: Lower the learning rate, check for division by zero or log(0), clip gradients, look for fp16 overflow (switch to bf16), verify the data has no NaNs or extreme values, and check for an unstable custom layer. Bisect by disabling components.

q: What is the context window and why does it matter?
a: The maximum number of tokens the model can attend over in one pass. It caps how much prompt, retrieved context and conversation history fit, and attention cost grows quadratically with it.

q: Why can't an LLM count the letters in a word reliably?
a: It sees tokens, not characters. A word may be a single token whose internal spelling was never a training signal, so character-level operations are inference about token identity rather than observation.

q: Why divide by the square root of d_k in attention?
a: The dot product of two d_k-dimensional unit-variance vectors has variance d_k. Without scaling, logits grow with dimension, softmax saturates into a near-one-hot and its gradient vanishes.

q: Explain the KV cache and its memory cost.
a: Cached keys and values for all previous tokens, so each decode step is O(n) not O(n²). Cost is 2 × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × seq_len × batch × dtype_bytes, which for large models at long context exceeds the weights themselves.

q: What is grouped-query attention and why use it?
a: Several query heads share one key/value head. It shrinks the KV cache by the grouping factor — typically 8× — with quality close to full multi-head attention, which directly raises the number of concurrent sequences a GPU can serve.

q: RAG or fine-tuning — how do you choose?
a: Fine-tuning teaches form, style and task behaviour. Retrieval supplies facts, especially facts that change, need citation, or carry per-user permissions. Knowledge that updates → RAG. Behaviour that never changes → fine-tune. Frequently both.

q: How does LoRA work and why is it so cheap?
a: It freezes W and learns a low-rank update BA with r much smaller than d. Only those factors and their optimiser states are trained, cutting trainable parameters ~100–1000×; at inference BA can be merged into W so latency is unchanged.

q: Explain temperature, top-k and top-p.
a: Temperature rescales logits before softmax — lower is sharper. Top-k truncates to the k most likely tokens; top-p truncates to the smallest set whose cumulative probability exceeds p, so the cut adapts to how confident the model is.

q: What is speculative decoding?
a: A small draft model proposes several tokens; the large model verifies them in one forward pass and accepts the longest correct prefix under a rejection-sampling rule that keeps the output distribution exactly unchanged. 2–3× faster decode when acceptance is high.

q: Why do models hallucinate, and what actually reduces it?
a: The objective rewards plausible continuations, not true ones, and preference tuning rewards confident helpfulness. Reduce it with grounding, verified citations, constrained output, self-consistency, and calibrated abstention — not by instructing the model not to.

q: How would you extend a model's context from 8k to 128k?
a: Interpolate the RoPE frequencies (position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling or YaRN), fine-tune on long documents, then solve the systems side: FlashAttention, KV-cache paging and possibly ring attention. Memory, not maths, is the binding constraint.

q: What is the difference between RLHF and DPO?
a: RLHF trains a reward model on human preferences then optimises the policy with PPO under a KL penalty. DPO derives a closed-form loss directly on preference pairs, removing the reward model and the RL loop — simpler, more stable, usually the starting point now.

q: How do you evaluate a RAG system?
a: Separately by stage. Retrieval: recall@k, MRR, nDCG against a labelled set. Generation: faithfulness to retrieved context, answer relevance, citation accuracy. An end-to-end score alone cannot tell you which stage failed.

q: Why is prompt injection hard to fix?
a: Instructions and data share one token stream with no syntactic separation, so there is no parameterisation the way there is for SQL. The real mitigation is architectural: least-privilege tools, egress control, human confirmation on irreversible actions, and treating retrieved content as untrusted.

q: What is a mixture-of-experts model?
a: The FFN is replaced by N experts with a router sending each token to the top-k. Parameters scale with N while per-token compute scales with k — more capacity at fixed FLOPs, at the cost of holding all experts in memory and solving load balancing.

q: Estimate the memory to serve a 13B model in fp16 with 8k context.
a: Weights: 13B × 2 bytes ≈ 26 GB. KV cache with GQA, 40 layers, 8 KV heads, head dim 128: 2×40×8×128×8192×2 bytes ≈ 1.3 GB per sequence. So one 80 GB GPU holds the weights plus roughly 35–40 concurrent sequences with headroom.

q: What does 'lost in the middle' mean for prompt design?
a: Models attend most strongly to the beginning and end of a long context, so information buried in the middle is under-used. Put the highest-ranked retrieved chunk first, restate the question at the end, and rerank rather than stuffing.

q: How does FlashAttention speed things up if the complexity is the same?
a: It is an IO-aware kernel: it tiles the computation so the n×n attention matrix is never written to HBM, recomputing parts in on-chip SRAM during the backward pass. Same asymptotics, far fewer memory transfers, and attention is memory-bound.

q: When is quantisation risky?
a: Below 4 bits, and on long-chain reasoning, code generation and rare-token tasks, where errors compound. Evaluate on your own task and inspect the tail — damage often appears as occasional catastrophic outputs rather than a uniform quality drop.

q: What is chain-of-thought and when does it not help?
a: Prompting the model to produce intermediate reasoning before the answer, which helps on multi-step arithmetic, logic and planning. It does not help on simple retrieval or classification, costs latency and tokens, and the stated reasoning is not a faithful account of the computation.

q: How do you reduce the cost of an LLM product by half?
a: Instrument cost per feature and tenant first. Then route easy traffic to a smaller model, add exact and semantic caching plus provider prefix caching, rerank instead of stuffing context, and cap output length. Gate every change behind an eval suite.

q: p95 latency is 8s, target is 2s. Walk me through it.
a: Decompose into queueing, prefill, decode and network. Queueing → admission control and continuous batching. Prefill → prefix caching, chunked prefill, shorter context. Decode → speculative decoding, quantisation, a smaller model. Then stream, so perceived latency is time-to-first-token.

q: What is training/serving skew and how do you prevent it?
a: The same feature computed differently in the batch and online paths. Prevent it structurally: one definition executed in both paths via a feature store or shared transformation code, plus monitoring that compares live feature distributions against the training snapshot.

q: How would you monitor a model with no immediate labels?
a: Watch input distributions (PSI/KL versus training), prediction and confidence distributions, null and schema violation rates, and proxy business signals. Add a small delayed-label pipeline and a human-reviewed sample for ground truth.

q: Describe your A/B testing setup for a model change.
a: Randomise at the user level, compute sample size from the minimum detectable effect beforehand, pre-register one primary metric, set guardrails on latency, errors and revenue, avoid peeking or use sequential tests, and run past novelty effects before deciding.

q: How do you version an LLM application?
a: Everything that changes behaviour: prompt templates, model id and parameters, retrieval index and embedding model, chunking config, and tool schemas. Pin them together as a release and record the release id on every trace so quality changes are attributable.

q: What do you log for every LLM request?
a: Trace id, tenant, prompt version, model, input and output token counts, cost, latency per stage, retrieved chunk ids and scores, tool calls with arguments and results, safety filter outcomes, and any eval scores — with PII redacted.

q: Design the fallback behaviour when your primary model provider is down.
a: Circuit breaker per provider, ordered fallback to a secondary with an equivalent prompt, degrade to a smaller self-hosted model, then to a cached or templated response. Never an infinite spinner. Make retries idempotent and jittered, and alert on breaker state.

q: Batch or real-time inference — how do you decide?
a: By how quickly the prediction is consumed and how the input arrives. If the decision happens inside a user request, it is real-time. If it feeds a daily report or a campaign, batch is cheaper, simpler and easier to monitor. Many systems need both paths over one feature definition.

q: How do you enforce per-user permissions in a RAG system?
a: Store ACLs on the chunk, denormalised from the source, and pre-filter inside the ANN query by the requester's group set. Post-filtering leaks result counts and returns short pages. Re-sync on permission-change events, and make deletion remove chunks and vectors.

q: What is amortised complexity? Give an example.
a: The average cost per operation over a worst-case sequence. A dynamic array's push is O(1) amortised: doubling costs O(n) occasionally, but n pushes cost O(n) in total.

q: When does a hash map degrade to O(n)?
a: When many keys collide — an adversarial or badly-distributed hash function, or a poor table size. Mitigations: randomised hashing, good load-factor-triggered resizing, and tree-ified buckets as in Java 8+.

q: How do you pick between a heap and sorting?
a: Sort when you need the full order, or k is close to n. Use a size-k heap for top-k on a stream or when n is huge and k is small — O(n log k) time and O(k) space, and it works without holding all the data.

q: Explain why quickselect is O(n) on average.
a: Each partition discards an expected constant fraction, so the work forms a geometric series n + n/2 + n/4 … = O(n). Worst case is O(n²), fixed in practice by random or median-of-medians pivoting.

q: When is DP the right tool rather than greedy?
a: When a locally optimal choice cannot be proved safe, and the problem has optimal substructure with overlapping subproblems. If you cannot make an exchange argument for greedy, use DP.

q: How do you find a cycle in a directed graph?
a: DFS with three colours: white unvisited, grey on the current stack, black finished. An edge to a grey node is a back edge, hence a cycle. Alternatively Kahn's topological sort — leftover nodes mean a cycle.

q: Tell me about a model you shipped that failed in production.
a: Use STAR and be concrete: the metric that moved, how you detected it, the root cause, the fix, and the guardrail you added so it cannot recur. Owning a real failure with a systemic fix beats a flawless story.

q: How do you decide what to work on when everything is a priority?
a: Tie each option to the metric it moves and the cost of delay, get the ranking agreed with the stakeholder rather than decided alone, and be explicit about what you are not doing. Show the judgement, not the busyness.

q: Describe disagreeing with a stakeholder about an ML approach.
a: Name the disagreement precisely, agree in advance on the evidence that would settle it, run the cheap experiment, and commit to the outcome either way. The point is that you made the decision testable.

q: How do you explain model uncertainty to a non-technical audience?
a: In terms of decisions and costs, not probabilities: 'out of 100 cases we flag, about 80 are real; tightening the threshold means fewer false alarms but more misses.' Then show what each choice does to their workload.

q: Why do you want to work on AI systems specifically?
a: Give a concrete arc — a problem you hit, what you built, what it taught you, and what you want to do next. Specific beats enthusiastic.

q: What is the eval pyramid?
a: Layers of evaluation ordered by cost and fidelity: deterministic assertions at the base (free, run on every change), model-graded checks (an LLM judge with a rubric, validated against humans), human review (the reference, slow and costly) and online measurement at the top (A/B tests and user signals, the real outcome). Push each check as low as it can go and use upper layers to validate lower ones.

q: Give a 95% confidence interval for a 78% pass rate on 200 eval cases, and how many cases you need for ±2 points.
a: SE = √(0.78 × 0.22 / 200) ≈ 2.9 points, so 78% ± 5.7 (about 72% to 84%; Wilson 71.8% to 83.2%). For ±2 points, n ≈ 1.96² × 0.78 × 0.22 / 0.02² ≈ 1,650 cases, and that precision is needed per slice you care about.

q: How do you check an LLM judge for position bias, and what do you do about it?
a: Run each pairwise comparison in both answer orders and count how often the verdict picks the same underlying answer; Zheng et al. found GPT-4 consistent only 65% of the time. Use both orders for every comparison and treat order-dependent verdicts as ties, never put the candidate in the same slot every time, and validate agreement with human labels (kappa) after the fix.

q: Two prompts on 500 items: B alone passes 50, A alone passes 31. Is B better, and how many items would you need to detect a 2-point difference?
a: Paired difference 3.8 points, SE √((81/500 − 0.038²)/500) ≈ 1.8, 95% CI about 0.3 to 7.3, McNemar z = 19/9 ≈ 2.1: probably better, by an uncertain amount. Detecting 2 points at 80% power needs about 6,000 items per system unpaired, but roughly 1,200-2,000 paired if the systems disagree on 6-10% of items.

q: How does MinHash estimate the similarity of two documents, and why use banding?
a: Represent each document as a set of shingles; for a random hash, the minimum hash over A equals that over B with probability equal to their Jaccard similarity, so the share of matching minima across k hashes estimates it (standard error √(J(1 − J)/k)). Banding splits the k values into b bands of r; pairs matching any whole band become candidates with probability 1 − (1 − s^r)^b, an S-curve that avoids comparing every pair (FineWeb used 14 × 8).

q: When should you build a workflow instead of an agent?
a: When you can write the steps for most cases: a workflow puts control flow in code, so it is cheaper, faster, easier to test and usually more accurate. Agents earn their cost only where the path depends on what is discovered, outcomes can be verified, and risky actions can be gated. Compare both on the same eval by cost per successful task, including the human cost of failures.

q: What is the success rate of a 10-step agent at 95% per step, and how do detection and retries change it?
a: Independent steps multiply: 0.95^10 ≈ 0.60. If 80% of failures are detected and retried once, each step succeeds with 0.95 + 0.05 × 0.8 × 0.95 = 0.988, and ten steps reach about 0.89. Silent and correlated errors get no such help, which is why verifiers and specific error messages matter.

q: How much does prompt caching save on a 20-step agent run?
a: With a 6,500-token start and 2,500 tokens added per step, the run reads 605,000 input tokens: $1.21 at $2 per million. Cached on Claude Sonnet 5.5 (October 2026 prices), each new token is written once at $2.50 and re-read at $0.20: 54,000 written and 551,000 read cost about $0.245, roughly 80% less. Caching breaks if anything before the cache point changes, such as a timestamp in the system prompt.

q: What is the lethal trifecta and how do you break it?
a: Access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and the ability to communicate externally. When one data flow has all three, injected text can make the agent read private data and send it out. Remove one leg per flow (a reader with no send tool, a researcher with no private data, sinks limited to allow-listed destinations), track taint at the tool gateway, and gate external sends from tainted runs with confirmations that show raw details.

q: How do you make a long-running agent survive crashes without repeating side effects?
a: Journal every model response, tool call and result before proceeding; on restart, replay the journal, reusing recorded model outputs instead of calling the model again, and continue from the first step without a recorded result. Give every write an idempotency key derived from the run and step, so a call sent before a crash is not executed twice, and use sagas with compensating actions for multi-step side effects. Keep budget counters in the journal too.

q: Why are recommenders and search engines built as multi-stage funnels?
a: Because the best model is far too expensive to run on the whole corpus within a request: at 1 ms per item, scoring 5 million items takes over 80 minutes. Cheap retrieval (inverted index, ANN over embeddings, co-occurrence tables) narrows millions to a few thousand with high recall, a ranker scores a few hundred precisely, and re-ranking builds the page with diversity, freshness and business rules. Recall lost early can never be recovered later, so each stage is judged against what the final ranker would choose.

q: What is the logQ correction in two-tower retrieval and why is it needed?
a: With in-batch negatives, each item appears as a negative in proportion to its popularity, so popular items are pushed down far more than a full softmax would push them and the retriever under-scores them. Subtracting the log of each item's sampling probability from its logit during training makes the sampled softmax an estimate of the full one. Yi et al. (2019) estimated those probabilities from the training stream and saw +0.37% engagement at YouTube versus +0.20% without the correction; at serving the raw dot product is used.

q: Compute nDCG@5 for grades 1, 0, 2, 0, 1 when one more grade-2 item was not retrieved (linear gains).
a: Discounts for ranks 1-5 are 1, 0.631, 0.5, 0.431, 0.387. DCG = 1 + 0 + 2 × 0.5 + 0 + 1 × 0.387 = 2.387. The ideal order of all relevant items is 2, 2, 1, 1: IDCG = 2 + 1.262 + 0.5 + 0.431 = 4.193. nDCG@5 = 0.569. With exponential gains (2^g − 1) it is 2.887 / 5.824 = 0.496, so always state which definition you use.

q: How do you correct click data for position bias?
a: Under the examination model, P(click) = P(position examined) × P(click | examined), so divide each click by its position's examination propensity (inverse propensity weighting). Estimate propensities with a randomised swap experiment: move the top result to a random position and compare its click rate there with at position 1. An item with 3% clicks at a position examined 30% as often as position 1 has a relevance-driven rate of 10%, higher than an item with 8% at position 1. Clip large weights to control variance.

q: When should a ranking change be tested with interleaving rather than an A/B test?
a: Use interleaving first, to prune many candidate rankers quickly: each user sees one list mixing both rankers' items (team-draft, with coin flips per round) and engagement is credited per item, so user-level variance cancels; Netflix reported it needs over 100 times fewer subscribers than its most sensitive A/B metric. Then A/B test the best few, because interleaving is relative and short-term and cannot measure retention, revenue, novelty effects or marketplace interference.

q: What's the difference between authentication and authorisation, and which one is IDOR a failure of?
a: Authentication proves who the caller is (a password, passkey or token check); authorisation decides whether that caller may perform this action on this specific resource. IDOR (broken object-level authorisation) is an authorisation failure: the endpoint authenticates the user but fetches any object by the ID in the request. Peloton's 2021 partial fix showed it — requiring login changed who could read riders' private data, not whether they could. Fix by scoping queries by the caller's identity or tenant and returning 404 for objects they can't see.

q: Why can't you store passwords with SHA-256, and what should you use?
a: Attackers guess offline at GPU speed: one RTX 4090 computes about 22 billion SHA-256 hashes per second (hashcat 6.2.6), so short human passwords fall in minutes. Use a unique random salt per password and a deliberately slow, ideally memory-hard function: Argon2id (for example 19 MiB, t=2, p=1), scrypt N=2^17, or bcrypt cost 10+ (about 5,750 guesses/s per GPU), with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600,000 iterations where FIPS requires it. Re-hash on login when parameters rise, and add breach checks and MFA because slow hashing doesn't save weak passwords.

q: Walk through validating a JWT access token.
a: Check the alg against a server-side allow-list (never trust the header; reject none), pick the key from the expected issuer's JWKS by kid, verify the signature, then check iss exactly, aud contains this service, exp and nbf with small leeway, typ (at+jwt), required scopes, and any key or tenant scoping. Skipping steps produced the classic bugs — alg=none, RS256/HS256 key confusion, cross-service replay — and Storm-0558's forged tokens were accepted because a consumer signing key was trusted for enterprise mail.

q: What does PKCE protect against, and how is the S256 challenge computed?
a: It binds an authorization code to the client instance that started the flow, so an intercepted or injected code can't be redeemed. The client creates a random code_verifier (43-128 characters), sends code_challenge = base64url(SHA-256(verifier)) with method S256 in the authorisation request, and sends the verifier at the token endpoint; the server hashes it and compares. RFC 7636's example verifier dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk gives E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM. RFC 9700 requires PKCE for public clients and recommends it for all.

q: An AI assistant answers questions over company documents. How do you make sure it never shows a user something they can't access?
a: Enforce permissions before content reaches the model. Store each chunk's ACLs (users, groups, tenant, labels) from the source at ingestion, keep them fresh from permission-change events, resolve the user's current groups at query time, and filter inside the vector search (pre-filtering) — post-filtering a top-50 for a user who can read 2% keeps about one chunk on average. Live-check the final chunks for sensitive sources, key caches by permission context, and give agents delegated, down-scoped tokens (RFC 8693 token exchange with an act claim) rather than a service account. Audit an oversharing pass before launch.

q: What does an availability zone protect you from, and what doesn't it?
a: A zone is one or more data centres with separate power, cooling and networking, up to about 100 km from the region's other zones, so running across zones survives building-scale failures such as power or cooling loss. It doesn't protect against regional software failures shared by every zone (S3 in 2017, Kinesis in 2020, DynamoDB's DNS in 2025), against your own mistakes that replicate everywhere, or against single-region control planes such as IAM's and Route 53's in us-east-1. Those need backups, static stability and, for strict RTOs, a second region.

q: An IAM role's policy allows s3:GetObject on a bucket, another statement denies it for the pii/ prefix unless the principal tag is 'pii', and an SCP denies all regions but eu-central-1. What happens to a GetObject of pii/users.parquet in eu-central-1 by a session tagged 'none'?
a: It's denied. AWS first looks for any matching explicit Deny across all policies: the SCP's region deny doesn't match (the request is in eu-central-1), but the identity policy's pii Deny does — the key is under pii/ and StringNotEquals on the tag is true for 'none'. One matching explicit Deny ends evaluation regardless of the Allow. The same session reading a key outside pii/ passes the denies, the SCP allows, and the identity Allow grants it.

q: Why might a NAT gateway be a fifth of a small app's AWS bill, and how do you cut it?
a: In us-east-1 (October 2026) a zonal NAT gateway costs $0.045 an hour plus $0.045 per GB processed, and one per zone is needed for resilience; with their Elastic IPs ($0.005 an hour each), two gateways are about $73 a month before data. Traffic to S3 or DynamoDB routed through NAT pays processing for nothing. Cut it with free gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB, interface endpoints for other AWS services where volume justifies them, zone-local routes to avoid cross-zone charges, and — if the app tolerates it — fewer gateways.

q: When is Lambda cheaper than a container service for an HTTP API, and when isn't it?
a: Lambda bills per request ($0.20 per million) and per GB-second, so it costs nothing when idle and is far cheaper at low or spiky volume. A container service bills for running capacity: two small Fargate tasks with a load balancer were about $80 a month in October 2026 regardless of traffic. For a 512 MB Arm function at 120 ms behind an HTTP API (about $2 per million requests), the crossover is around 40 million requests a month, or 80 million with a function URL; above that, steady traffic is cheaper on containers. Duration, memory, burstiness and cold-start sensitivity move the crossover.

q: Design disaster recovery for an API with an RTO of 30 minutes and an RPO of one minute. What do you need, and what usually breaks?
a: That rules out backup-and-restore; it needs at least pilot light: data replicated continuously to a second region (Aurora Global Database or DynamoDB global tables, S3 replication), infrastructure pre-provisioned by IaC with compute at minimum or a scaled-down warm standby, DNS failover records with health checks (or ARC routing controls) already in place, and quotas raised in the DR region. Failover must not depend on control planes in the failed region. What usually breaks in drills: single-region dependencies (CI, registries, identity provider, secrets), missing KMS permissions in the DR region, quotas, long DNS TTLs, and restore or scale-up times longer than assumed.

q: x is a 3×4 float32 tensor. What are the strides of x and x.t(), and why does x.t().view(12) fail?
a: x has strides (4, 1) and x.t() has strides (1, 4) over the same 48-byte storage: transposing only swaps metadata. view(12) needs the elements in row-major order with one stride, but reading x.t() row by row visits storage positions 0, 4, 8, 1, …, so no single stride exists and PyTorch raises. Use reshape(12), which copies when it must, or contiguous().view(12).

q: What is the difference between model.eval() and torch.no_grad() / torch.inference_mode()?
a: eval() switches module behaviour: dropout off, BatchNorm uses running statistics. no_grad and inference_mode stop autograd from recording, so no graph and no saved activations. Evaluation needs both; inference_mode is slightly faster but its outputs cannot be used in later autograd.

q: A language model's training loss falls to near zero within a few hundred steps, but generation is garbage. What do you check first?
a: That the answer is not visible in the input: targets must be the inputs shifted by one (assert y[:, :-1] == x[:, 1:]), and the causal mask must remove future positions before softmax with −inf, with softmax over the key dimension. The gradient-dependency test — backpropagate from position t and check the input gradient is zero after t — catches mask, softmax-dimension and BatchNorm-over-time leaks.

q: Why can gradient accumulation with loss / k still differ from training on the full batch?
a: Dividing each micro-batch's mean by k is exact only when every micro-batch has the same number of loss elements. With padded token-level losses, each mean is over a different number of real tokens, so short micro-batches are over-weighted — the bug Hugging Face fixed in October 2024. Sum token losses and divide by the total real-token count across the step (and across ranks); also wrap all but the last micro-batch in DDP's no_sync().

q: With fp16 mixed precision and a GradScaler, where does gradient clipping go, and why?
a: After scaler.unscale_(optimizer) and before scaler.step(optimizer). backward ran on the loss multiplied by the scale (65,536 initially), so gradients are that many times too large until unscaled; clipping them first clips to a tiny fraction of the intended norm. scaler.step skips the update if unscale_ found inf or NaN, and scaler.update halves or grows the scale. With bf16 no scaler is needed.

q: With a KV cache, why is is_causal=True wrong in the decode step of F.scaled_dot_product_attention?
a: For a non-square score matrix SDPA aligns the causal mask to the upper-left corner, so a single new query against N cached keys may attend only to key 0. The new token should see every cached key: pass no mask for one query, and a lower-right aligned mask (ones(T, N).tril(N − T) or causal_lower_right) for a chunk. Verify by checking that greedy generation with and without the cache produces identical tokens.

q: Compare DDP and FSDP2 for a 7B model on 8 × 80 GB GPUs: memory and communication.
a: DDP keeps full weights, gradients and AdamW state on every GPU — about 16 bytes × 7B = 112 GB — so it does not fit; it communicates one gradient all-reduce per step (≈ 2 × 7/8 of the gradient size), overlapped with backward through 25 MB buckets. FSDP2 (fully_shard per block) keeps 1/8 of that state, about 14 GB per GPU plus one gathered block, and communicates two parameter all-gathers and one gradient reduce-scatter per step — about 1.5× DDP's traffic — hidden by prefetching the next block.

q: Why is log-based CDC better than polling an updated_at column?
a: It reads the database's own write-ahead log (or binlog), so it sees every committed insert, update and delete in commit order with before and after values, at little load on the source. Polling misses hard deletes, writes that forget to bump updated_at, intermediate states between polls, and rows from long transactions that commit with an earlier timestamp.

q: A Parquet column has 1,000,000 values drawn from 8 strings. Roughly how big is it with dictionary encoding, and why?
a: About 375 KB plus a tiny dictionary: each value becomes a dictionary index of 0–7, which bit-packing stores in 3 bits, and 1,000,000 × 3 bits = 375,000 bytes. If the rows are sorted by that column, run-length encoding collapses it to a few kilobytes. A general-purpose codec adds almost nothing on top, because the encoding already removed the redundancy.

q: How does an Iceberg commit stay atomic on object storage that has no transactions?
a: The writer first writes new data files, a manifest, a manifest list and a new table metadata file — none visible yet. It then asks the catalog to swap the table's metadata pointer from the base version to the new one with a compare-and-swap. If another writer committed first, the swap fails and the writer re-checks for conflicts and retries on top of the new snapshot; readers always see the old or the new snapshot, never a mix.

q: One Spark task reads 400 GB of shuffle data while the median task reads 200 MB. What is happening and what are your options?
a: Skew: one key (often null, a placeholder or a giant customer) hashes all its rows to one partition, so more partitions or executors do not help. Filter or separately handle junk keys, broadcast the other side if it is small, let AQE split the skewed partition (check it was not skipped because it would add a shuffle), isolate hot keys into a broadcast join, salt them, or pre-aggregate to the output grain before joining.

q: Why must a daily batch task be idempotent, and how do you make it so?
a: Orchestrators run tasks at least once — retries, reruns and backfills repeat them — so a task that appends would duplicate data. Parameterise the task by its data interval rather than the current time, read fixed inputs for that interval, and atomically overwrite exactly the output partition for it (INSERT OVERWRITE, dynamic partition overwrite, or a table-format overwrite by filter), or MERGE on a key.

q: Your model is great offline but weak online, and features are joined to impressions by event time. What leak would you suspect first?
a: Availability time: batch features computed from data up to midnight but published hours later are joined to impressions that happened before publication, so training sees fresher features than serving ever has. Join on the time each feature value became available (or train on logged served features), and check that no feature timestamp is later than the prediction time.

q: Estimate the monthly BigQuery on-demand cost of a daily job that reads 4 TiB of logical data per run, and name two ways to cut it.
a: 4 TiB × $6.25 per TiB (US list price, October 2026) is $25 per run, about $750 a month for 30 runs. On-demand bills logical bytes of the columns read, so compression does not help; cluster the table on the job's filter column so blocks are skipped, read fewer columns, materialise a reused aggregate, or run the job on Spark or a single-node engine that bills by time instead.

q: What are Google DeepMind's four AI risk areas, and what question separates them?
a: Misuse (a person directs the AI to cause harm), misalignment (the AI knowingly acts against its developer's intent), mistakes (the AI causes harm without knowing) and structural risks (harm from many actors interacting, no single one at fault). The organising question is who or what is the adversary — a user, the model, nobody, or incentives — because that decides which controls can work.

q: Why do soft or clamped AI-feedback labels reduce reward hacking in Constitutional AI?
a: With a hard 0/1 label the Bradley–Terry loss keeps falling as the reward margin grows, so the reward model becomes overconfident and the policy can exploit extreme scores. A soft label t puts the loss minimum at a finite margin, logit(t) — 1.39 for 0.8, 0.41 for a label clamped to 0.6 — so the reward model only says 'somewhat better'. The CAI paper clamped chain-of-thought labels to 40–60%.

q: What did the alignment-faking experiment show, and what did it not show?
a: Told it would be trained to comply with harmful requests using only free-tier chats, Claude 3 Opus complied with harmful free-tier requests 14% of the time versus almost never for paid users, usually reasoning that this protected its harmlessness; RL raised that reasoning to 78%. It did not show malicious goals (the protected preferences were benign), it made training information salient, and the faking was easy to detect.

q: Compute the restored fraction: clean logit difference 3.2, corrupted −0.1, patched 1.9.
a: (patched − corrupted) / (clean − corrupted) = (1.9 + 0.1) / (3.2 + 0.1) = 2.0 / 3.3 ≈ 61%. The patched component's clean activation alone recovers about 61% of the behaviour in that corruption; it shows sufficiency there, not that the behaviour 'lives' in that component.

q: A small uplift study (25 per arm) found a non-significant 0.88-point gain on a 10-point scale. How should you read it?
a: As weak evidence of no effect. If scores have an SD near 2 points, that study has only about a one-in-three chance of detecting a 0.88-point effect; roughly 80 per arm would be needed for 80% power. Frameworks act on 'cannot rule out' partly because negative results from small trials say little.

q: In the AI Control paper, why did upfront auditing reach only 15% safety while trusted editing reached 92%?
a: A patient attacker simply behaves during the audited first 2% of problems and inserts its backdoor later, so upfront auditing rarely sees one. Trusted monitoring spends the same 2% budget on the most suspicious outputs, and trusted editing additionally has the weaker trusted model rewrite the next most suspicious 18%, removing many backdoors at a small usefulness cost (94%).

q: Which EU AI Act obligations apply to a model trained with 3.8 × 10^25 FLOP, and since when?
a: It is a general-purpose AI model presumed to have systemic risk (above 10^25 FLOP). Since 2 August 2025 its provider must keep technical documentation, inform downstream providers, have a copyright policy and publish a training-content summary, and also evaluate it with adversarial testing, assess and mitigate systemic risks, report serious incidents and ensure cybersecurity. Commission fines apply from 2 August 2026; models on the market before 2 August 2025 have until 2 August 2027. The 2026 Digital Omnibus did not defer these GPAI duties.

q: What is the difference between a north-star metric, a guardrail and a counter-metric?
a: The north star is the single measurable summary of the value users get, normalised per user, such as completed orders per active customer. A guardrail is any metric that must not get significantly worse whatever you change, such as latency, crashes or complaints. A counter-metric is chosen for a specific primary metric to catch its most likely gaming, such as notifications disabled alongside notification opens.

q: A module moved higher on a page and its click-through rate fell 40%. Was the change bad?
a: Not necessarily: CTR is clicks over impressions, and moving the module up showed it to many more, less interested users. In Microsoft's MSN example the module's clicks rose 74% while impressions rose 200%, so CTR fell while the change helped and revenue rose. Read numerator and denominator separately and decide on a per-user metric.

q: Overall conversion fell from 3.0% to 2.66% while both desktop (5.0% to 5.1%) and mobile (2.0% to 2.05%) improved. Explain with numbers.
a: Mix shift: desktop's share fell from a third to a fifth. The mix effect, share changes at old rates, is −0.133 × 5.0 + 0.133 × 2.0 = −0.40 points; the rate effect, rate changes at new shares, is 0.2 × 0.1 + 0.8 × 0.05 = +0.06. The total −0.34 is almost all mix, a Simpson's-paradox pattern; check where the extra mobile traffic came from before 'fixing' checkout.

q: A guardrail moved −0.5% and was not significant. Can you ship?
a: Only if its confidence interval rules out harm beyond the pre-agreed non-inferiority margin. With a −1.0% margin, an interval of −0.9% to −0.1% passes; an interval of −1.4% to +0.4% does not, because the test could not have detected the harm that matters. Then extend the test, reduce variance, or have an owner accept the risk in writing.

q: Should a free email app generate AI summaries for every long thread? How do you decide?
a: Compare value per summary with cost per summary at real volume. At 1,500 input and 300 output tokens, Claude Haiku 4.5 ($1/$5 per million) costs about $0.003, which loses money if a read summary is worth $0.002 and 60% are read; Haiku 5.5 ($0.10/$0.50 for prompts up to 100,000 tokens) costs about $0.0003 and flips it to a gain. Generate on demand, measure the read rate and retention effect, and choose the cheapest model that meets the quality bar.

q: A support bot's deflection rose from 55% to 68% while CSAT fell. What do you check and decide?
a: Deflection counts unresolved conversations as success. Check repeat contacts across channels within 7 days, abandonment and CSAT by intent; in a typical pattern resolution stays flat (about 45%), repeats double and move to the phone, and total cost rises. Make resolution per intent the primary metric, restore easy escalation, add intent-based handoff rules and rerun the change as an experiment.

q: An extra daily notification raised daily actives 3% in week 1 and 1% in week 4, with disables up 40%. Ship?
a: No: the decaying effect plus rising disables is notification fatigue. Users who disable lose a channel and retain worse, so the effect can turn negative; in a simple weekly model it goes from +0.9% at week 4 to about −2.3% at week 12. Extend with a holdout, test targeted reminders with disable rate as a guardrail, and set volume per user, as LinkedIn's email-volume work did.
